fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: The Velocity Trap
fieldNotes.source: Anonymous APM at Skytrip, a Bengaluru-based travel SaaS (Series A, ~120 staff)
fieldNotes.story:
On March 4, 2025, Skytrip's engineering lead pinged the new APM, Aditya, on Slack: *"We can ship a redesigned booking-confirmation page in one sprint — three engineers are unblocked. Want it?"*

Aditya, eight days into the job and desperate to look decisive, said yes. He wrote a half-page brief on Tuesday, design landed Wednesday, code merged Friday. The team shipped a beautiful new confirmation page on **March 21**. It had a nicer hero image, a clearer trip summary, and a 'share with co-traveller' button engineering had been wanting to build for months.

Three weeks of analytics later: **0.4%** of confirmed bookings used the share button. The 'nicer' confirmation page had no measurable lift on repeat-booking rate. The actual top-3 customer complaints — slow refunds, confusing baggage rules, no IRCTC fallback when flights got cancelled — were untouched.

In the post-mortem, the engineering lead said the quiet part out loud: *"We had bandwidth and a feature we wanted to build. You said go."* Aditya had optimised for **shipping** when his job was to optimise for **users not getting screwed on refunds**. The roadmap lost a sprint. The customers lost six more weeks.
fieldNotes.takeaway: An engineering team with bandwidth is not a customer with a problem. The PM's job is to know the difference — and say no when it isn't.

bossBattle.title: Boss Battle: Rhea's First Monday
bossBattle.setup:
It's **Monday, week 1** at Tarakash, a 200-person Bengaluru B2B SaaS. **Rhea** has been an APM for exactly 4 working days. At 9:47am, the CEO forwards her an email with a one-line note: *"Pls handle. Need response by EOD."*

The email is from **Mehta & Co.**, Tarakash's third-largest customer (₹38L ARR, renewal in 11 weeks). Their ops head writes: *"Your team takes 3 days to respond to support tickets. Our compliance officer needs SLA dashboards visible in the product. Please add this. Otherwise we may not renew."*

Rhea's Slack lights up. The engineering lead, Shankar, has already replied to a separate thread saying: *"We can spin up a basic SLA dashboard in 2 sprints if we cut the search-relevance work."* Rhea has 7 hours and one shot to respond.

coach.name: Director-PM Devika
coach.role: Director of Product, Tarakash · 11 years in product, allergic to feature requests dressed as ultimatums

stages.prompt: Devika DMs Rhea: *"Before you reply to anyone — what's the actual problem here?"* What do you have Rhea say back?

options.label: "The problem is Mehta wants an SLA dashboard. I'll scope it with Shankar."
options.explain: You restated the **output** as the problem. Devika sighs. The customer asked for a dashboard, but the underlying complaint is *3-day support response times*. A dashboard makes slow support **visible**, not faster. You're about to spend two sprints decorating a wound.

options.label: "The problem is our support is slow. The dashboard is their proposed fix. I want to verify the response-time number before agreeing to anything."
options.explain: **Yes.** Outcome (fast support) vs output (dashboard) cleanly separated, and you're going to check the data before you commit eng time. Devika sends back a thumbs-up and the world's smallest filter coffee emoji.

options.label: "The problem is Mehta is threatening to churn. We need to keep them happy, so let's ship the dashboard."
options.explain: Churn risk is real, but "keep customer happy" is a feeling, not a problem statement. You're about to pull two engineers off search-relevance to build a dashboard that may not move the renewal needle one millimetre. Re-read the lesson on **outcome vs output**.

options.label: "The problem is the CEO forwarded this to me, so I need to deliver something visible by EOD."
options.explain: Honest but wrong. If the only signal you optimise for is *"the CEO is watching me"*, you'll ship CEO-pleasing features for the rest of your career. Devika has seen this movie. It does not end well.

stages.prompt: Rhea pulls the support data. Median first-response time across all customers: **9 hours**. For Mehta specifically: **2.6 days** — because three of their tickets last month were tagged as 'feature request' and routed to the product backlog where they sat. What's Rhea's next move?

options.label: Reply to Mehta: "You're right, support is slow. We're shipping an SLA dashboard in 2 sprints."
options.explain: You confirmed the wrong cause. The median is fine — Mehta's specific tickets got mis-routed. A dashboard won't fix routing. You're treating an org problem with a UI bandage and burning engineers in the process.

options.label: Reply to Mehta: "The 3-day delay was a routing bug specific to your account — we're fixing the routing this week. We'll also share weekly SLA numbers in your QBR. Holding off on a dashboard until we know it's the bottleneck."
options.explain: **This is the move.** Acknowledge the pain, name the actual cause, ship the cheap fix now, and **resist the expensive fix until proven necessary**. You also bought time to validate whether a dashboard is the right answer. Devika literally claps once.

options.label: Loop in Shankar and start scoping the dashboard while also fixing the routing bug. Cover both bases.
options.explain: "Both bases" sounds responsible and is actually how PMs ship 40% more work for 5% more outcome. You haven't validated that the dashboard is needed at all. Half-credit for fixing the routing.

options.label: Forward the data to the CEO and ask what to do.
options.explain: You escalated a decision that's literally your job. The CEO forwarded this to you because they wanted **a PM to decide**. Devika notes: "If you bounce every hard call back up, you're a forwarding service, not a PM."

stages.prompt: Mehta replies, mollified but still cranky: *"Fine. But we want SLA visibility within 90 days, dashboard or otherwise."* It's now 4:30pm. How does Rhea close the loop with the CEO?

options.label: "Handled. Mehta's happy. Routing fix shipping this week."
options.explain: Too thin. The CEO doesn't know what changed, why, or what trade-off you protected. In two weeks when this comes up in a board call, the CEO has nothing to say. Half a job.

options.label: Three lines: (1) Root cause was a ticket-routing bug, not a dashboard gap. (2) Routing fix this week, weekly SLA numbers in their QBR. (3) Did NOT pull eng off search-relevance — happy to revisit in 30 days if the metric doesn't move.
options.explain: **Beautiful.** Diagnosis, action, trade-off you protected, and a built-in review date. The CEO now trusts you with the next escalation instead of micro-managing it. Devika forwards your message to the rest of the PM team as 'how to write up an escalation.'

options.label: A 600-word document with a Gantt chart, three risk scenarios, and a stakeholder map.
options.explain: The CEO will not read 600 words. You optimised for looking thorough rather than being clear. The signal-to-noise ratio of a good PM update is high. Yours is currently low.

options.label: "Resolved for now. I'll keep an eye on it."
options.explain: Vague. "Keep an eye on it" is the PM equivalent of *"we'll circle back."* The CEO has no idea whether you fixed something, dodged something, or merely promised something. Trust isn't built on vibes.

outcomes.perfect: First Monday and you didn't ship a vanity feature, didn't pull engineers off real work, and wrote an escalation summary your CEO will quote. Devika quietly bumps you up the trust ladder. **Welcome to the job, Rhea.**
outcomes.good: You avoided the worst trap (shipping the dashboard reflexively) but stumbled on either the diagnosis or the wrap-up. Re-read the **outcome vs output** section before week 2 — the next escalation is already in someone's drafts folder.
outcomes.learn: You optimised for looking responsive instead of being effective. Re-read the lesson on **what a PM is actually for** — especially the bit on customer requests being hypotheses, not specs. Good news: you have 89 more days in your first 90.
